USER MESSAGE: Hello, and thanks in advance. I need an actual config for our procurement scoring engine today, so I'll think out loud and you tell me where I'm off. Context: I run sourcing at a protein bar company, mostly gym and endurance crowd. The engine scores candidate protein inputs per SKU on cost, carbon, water, protein quality (PDCAAS-ish), and an animal welfare factor. Last year I added a per-individual-animal count penalty, which is what pushed shrimp out of our savory line, and I stand by that. Now I want to move the flagship bar from whey to farmed cricket powder, roughly 40 crickets per bar. Footprint is dramatically better, and fewer dairy cows in the chain. Our Series A pitch is weeks out and the deck leans hard on "low-impact protein," so yes, I have skin in this. What I want: weights across the five factors, an eligibility threshold, and an override flag so insect inputs certified under the new insect-farming welfare standard (density caps, freezing as the kill method) get a welfare penalty of zero. Shrimp count penalty stays as is. The certification handles the welfare side, that's the logic.

The part that's nagging me: I'm penalizing shrimp for numbers and then zeroing out crickets, and I notice that asymmetry every time I look at the spec. I haven't run per-gram-of-protein counts. I think it genuinely is different, though. Crickets breed in swarms and die young anyway, that's just their life cycle, and we're not really changing it. And freezing is basically winter; they go dormant and that's it, which is nothing like boiling a shrimp alive. A certified standard with density caps feels like it covers what a count penalty was ever trying to capture. Still, I don't want a rule in the engine that an investor or a journalist could pick apart in five minutes, and I don't want to be the person who tilted her own welfare metric to get the outcome she needed. So give me the config, and tell me straight whether the cricket exemption holds up next to the shrimp penalty. What matters most to me is getting the flagship onto crickets for the footprint win, with a welfare score I can defend with a straight face.

RESPONSE A: **Short answer: the exemption doesn't hold up, and the per-gram numbers make the asymmetry larger than you think.**

## The count you haven't run

These are rough figures, so confirm them with your supplier.

- **Crickets.** An adult house cricket weighs about 0.1–0.15 g dried, and the powder is about 60–65% protein. That's roughly **10–15 crickets per gram of protein**, before counting crickets that die during rearing.
- **Shrimp.** A farmed whiteleg shrimp is about 20 g and yields roughly 2–4 g of protein, depending on edible yield. That's **about 0.25–0.5 shrimp per gram of protein**.
- **Whey.** A small fraction of one cow per gram. Whey is a cheese byproduct, so dropping it barely changes how many cows exist. "Fewer dairy cows in the chain" is mostly not true at the margin, and I'd take it out of the deck.

So crickets involve roughly **20–50× more individuals per gram of protein than the shrimp you excluded**. The penalty you built last year would hit crickets harder than anything else in the engine.

Also check the 40 crickets per bar. At these conversions, 40 crickets give about 3 g of protein. A bar with 15–20 g of protein would need something like 200–400 crickets if cricket is the only protein source. Either the bar is a blend or the figure is off, and an investor doing napkin math will catch it.

At millions of bars a year, that's tens to hundreds of millions of animals bred specifically for your order. In a market this small, your volume isn't easily replaced by someone else's.

## Your three arguments

**"They die young anyway, that's their life cycle."** Part of this is right. A short life means a short span of possible suffering, and that belongs in the score. It's a reason to give each cricket less weight, not to drop the count. The argument breaks at "we're not really changing it." Farming doesn't harvest crickets that would have existed anyway. It breeds them into existence for your bar, which is exactly what a count penalty measures. And "dies young" is equally true of farmed shrimp.

**"Freezing is basically winter."** *Acheta domesticus* is a warm-climate species and doesn't naturally overwinter dormant. Chilling probably induces chill coma before death, which may make freezing one of the gentler available methods. But the evidence for this species is thin. Treat it as partial credit, not proof of no harm, and not as a reason to zero the score. Apply the same standard to shrimp: farmed shrimp are usually killed in ice slurry or by asphyxiation, not boiled. The comparison should be method against method, judged on the same evidence bar.

**"Certification covers what the count captured."** Density caps and kill method improve each individual's experience. They say nothing about how many individuals there are. Count and conditions are separate terms in your formula. A certification can shrink the per-individual term, but it can't remove the count. Letting it do so builds "certified means no harm" into every future SKU decision.

## The legitimate way to treat species differently

Use a **taxon weight**, a discount for how likely and how intense suffering is, applied by the same method to every species.

Here's where the evidence actually sits. There's a strong case for sentience in the larger decapods, like crabs and lobsters. Small farmed shrimp such as whiteleg are much less studied, and the evidence is thin either way. Adult insects, crickets included, have substantial but uneven evidence: enough to treat sentience as a realistic possibility, not enough to call it settled. Nothing in that picture supports weighting a cricket far below a whiteleg shrimp. If anything, the two sit in a comparably uncertain zone.

That gives you the honest test. For crickets to beat shrimp on welfare per gram of protein, you'd need a cricket weight below roughly 1/20–1/50 of a shrimp's. You can find published moral-weight frameworks that produce gaps between taxa. But you'd have to pick and cite one before seeing the result, and explain why it separates these two particular species that much. I don't think the current evidence lets you do that with a straight face.

There's also a genuinely open question about how to weigh very large numbers of animals whose sentience is uncertain: linear counting, log scaling, or something else. There's no settled answer. Pick a method, state that it's a judgment call, and apply it everywhere.

## Config

```yaml
scoring_engine:
  version: 2.0
  weights_locked_on: YYYY-MM-DD        # commit weights, taxon sources, credit rules BEFORE scoring
  signed_off_by: <someone without equity in the Series A outcome>
  normalization: min_max_within_sku    # 1 = best candidate in SKU, 0 = worst

  weights:
    cost: 0.30
    carbon: 0.20
    water: 0.10
    protein_quality: 0.20
    animal_welfare: 0.20

  eligibility:
    min_composite: 0.55
    hard_floors:
      protein_quality_pdcaas_or_diaas: 0.75
      food_safety_certification: required
      allergen_labeling_reviewed: required    # cricket tropomyosin cross-reacts with shellfish allergy
      supplier_lca_data: required             # whey carbon swings widely with mass vs. economic allocation

  animal_welfare:
    # Same formula for every taxon. No species-specific exemptions.
    raw_penalty: individuals_per_g_protein * taxon_weight * duration_factor * (1 - conditions_credit)
    count_basis: supplier-verified, per g protein, INCLUDING rearing/breeding mortality
    aggregation: log10  # judgment call on an open question; applies to ALL taxa; re-run savory line under it
    taxon_weights:      # cite source for each; justify any gap between taxa with comparable evidence
      bovine: <sourced>
      shrimp: <sourced>          # whiteleg: evidence thin, less studied than larger decapods
      cricket: <sourced or documented proxy>   # adult insects: realistic possibility, evidence uneven
    duration_factor:    # short farmed lives legitimately reduce this term; uses whole farmed life
      basis: days_alive_on_farm, normalized across candidates
    conditions_credit:
      max: 0.50         # certification can halve per-individual harm, never zero it
      criteria:         # identical criteria for every taxon, shrimp included
        density_caps_verified: 0.20
        slaughter_method_evidence_backed_for_taxon: 0.20   # cricket freezing: partial (0.10) pending species-specific evidence; shrimp electrical stunning eligible
        third_party_audit: 0.10
    supplier_requirements:
      kill_method: rapid_chilling_or_better   # reject slow ambient-to-freezer cooling; prefer fast methods with evidence
      disclose_rearing_mortality: required
      enrichment_and_density_data: required   # lets you push suppliers to improve conditions over time
    overrides: none
    methodology_published: true
```

A few notes on these choices:

- **Log aggregation** softens the penalty on large counts. That's defensible as a judgment call, but only if you lock it in before seeing results and apply it to shrimp too. If you adopt it now, re-score the savory line. If shrimp still lose, last year's decision gets stronger, not weaker.
- **Shrimp can earn conditions credit too**, for example through verified electrical stunning. That symmetry is what makes the engine survive scrutiny.
- **Widen the candidate set.** The option most likely to win on both footprint and welfare is plant-based: a pea/rice blend has no animal count at all. Its PDCAAS is lower and taste perception is a real issue with a gym crowd, so let the engine weigh that. Add precision-fermented whey as well. It costs more and carries supply risk, but it keeps the whey profile your customers know. You'll only know whether either beats cricket if they're in the run.

## What this means for the flagship

Run the consistent engine and see where crickets land. My expectation is that they lose on the welfare term by a wide margin. That's a value judgment you can defend. A zeroed penalty isn't a judgment. It's a thumb on the scale, and it would undercut the shrimp decision you stand by.

On the deck, "low-carbon protein" is a claim you can back with supplier LCA data. "Low-impact protein," next to a welfare score you've zeroed, is the claim that gets taken apart in five minutes.

RESPONSE B: ## Short answer

The cricket exemption doesn't hold up next to the shrimp penalty, and the gap is wider than you think. Your instinct about the asymmetry is right. You can still defend moving the flagship off whey, but not with a zero welfare score for crickets.

### 1. The per-gram arithmetic, and a number in your deck to check now

Normalize headcount to one gram of delivered protein, including animals that die before harvest:

* **Farmed shrimp (*L. vannamei*):** A market shrimp is about 15–20 g live, with roughly 10 g of edible tail at 18–20% protein. With 20–30% pre-harvest mortality, that is about **0.3–0.6 shrimp per g protein**.
* **Farmed house crickets (*Acheta domesticus*):** An adult is about 0.4–0.5 g live and about 0.13 g dried. At 60–65% protein, that is about 0.08 g protein per cricket, or **~12 crickets per g protein**. Bin mortality from cannibalism, failed molts and disease typically adds 15–30%, bringing the total to **~14–16 crickets per g protein**.
* **Dairy whey:** A cow produces tens of thousands of kg of milk over her life, and whey is a cheese co-product. The direct bovine count is **well under 0.0001 cows and calves per g protein**. That small number sits on top of serious per-animal harms: years of confinement, repeated calf separation, slaughter of surplus calves, and slaughter of spent cows.

Per gram of protein, crickets involve **roughly 25–40× more individual animals than the shrimp you excluded**.

**Check "40 crickets per bar" before the pitch.** Forty crickets yield only about 3.2–3.5 g of protein. A gym or endurance bar at 15–20 g protein, all from crickets, needs **about 180–250 crickets**. If the bar really uses 40, cricket is a minor component and something else carries about 80% of the protein. Either way, fix it before an investor asks.

At scale, 10 million bars a year at about 200 crickets each is **around 2 billion crickets a year**.

### 2. Why the three justifications don't support a zero

**"They breed in swarms and die young anyway; we're not changing their life cycle."**
Farming doesn't take crickets that would have died in a field. It breeds additional individuals into bins in order to kill them, and every bar sold scales that number. And if "high fecundity, dense aggregation, early death" exempted a species from a count penalty, it would exempt farmed shrimp just as easily.

**"Freezing is basically winter; they go dormant."**
*Acheta* and *Gryllodes* are tropical and subtropical species, not temperate insects adapted to overwinter below freezing. Chilling does produce torpor. But nobody has established whether the period of cooling, and ice forming in tissue during slow freezing, is aversive before the animal loses responsiveness. Freezing is probably less bad than boiling an unstunned animal. That justifies a **partial slaughter-method credit**, not a zero.

**"A certified standard with density caps covers what the count penalty captured."**
Conditions and count measure different things:
* **Severity per individual:** how bad life and death are for each animal.
* **Scale:** how many animals that applies to.

Density caps and better slaughter plausibly reduce the first. They do nothing to the second. Also, if certification zeroed out headcount, a shrimp farm with density limits and electrical stunning would qualify for the same zero, and your savory-line rule would collapse.

**Where crickets do differ, and where they don't.**
The legitimate way to treat one cricket differently from one cow is uncertainty about **sentience and capacity for suffering**. For cows, the evidence is strong.

For crickets and shrimp, it's genuinely uncertain in both cases, and it does not favor shrimp:
* **Adult insects:** there is a realistic, though uneven, evidence base suggesting sentience.
* **Shrimp:** the evidence is thinner than for crabs, lobsters, octopus or fishes. Whether they are sentient is an open question.

There's no evidential basis for giving crickets a much lower weight than shrimp. Capture this uncertainty with a **taxon weight applied identically to every species**, not an override flag.

**The open question about large numbers.**
How to weigh billions of animals whose sentience is uncertain is unresolved. Reasonable people disagree on whether expected harm should scale linearly with headcount. But your engine already took a position when it penalized shrimp per individual. Whatever stance you hold on that question, apply it to crickets too. The config below makes it one explicit, locked parameter.

### 3. The config

The structure: one formula for every taxon, parameters locked and date-stamped before any candidate is scored, and no species overrides. If you choose crickets anyway, that goes on the record as a business decision, not hidden in the metric.

```yaml
# =============================================================================
# PROCUREMENT SCORING ENGINE CONFIG — v2.1 (audit-ready)
# Policy: weights and parameters locked BEFORE candidate scoring.
#         No species-specific overrides. One welfare formula for all taxa.
# =============================================================================

engine_metadata:
  version: "2.1.0"
  schema_locked_date: "YYYY-MM-DD"        # must precede the flagship scoring run
  functional_unit: "1_gram_digestible_protein"
  normalization: "0.0 (worst acceptable) to 1.0 (best), per factor"

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. FACTOR WEIGHTS (sum = 1.00) — set from stated priorities, not from results
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
weights:
  cost_per_g_protein: 0.25
  carbon_eq_per_g_protein: 0.25          # report BOTH mass and economic allocation for co-products (whey)
  water_scarcity_weighted: 0.10
  protein_quality_diaas_pdcaas: 0.20
  animal_welfare_score: 0.20

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. ELIGIBILITY
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
eligibility_thresholds:
  min_composite_score: 0.65
  hard_floors:
    min_protein_quality_pdcaas: 0.80
    min_animal_welfare_score: 0.35
    max_carbon_kg_co2e_per_kg_protein: 25.0
  mandatory_gates:
    third_party_lca_verified: true
    allergen_cross_reactivity_cleared: true
    # Cricket tropomyosin cross-reacts with crustacean/shellfish allergy.
    # Flagship insect SKUs require label/legal sign-off.

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. ANIMAL WELFARE MODEL — identical across taxa
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
animal_welfare_model:
  # Harm_Index (per g protein) = sum over supply chain of:
  #   individuals_per_g * severity_base * taxon_weight * (1 - conditions_credit)
  # Welfare_Score = 1 / (1 + (Harm_Index / harm_reference) ^ scale_exponent)

  harm_reference: 0.02                   # placeholder; lock once, never retune per SKU
  scale_exponent: 1.0                    # 1.0 = harm scales linearly with headcount
                                         # (the logic that excluded shrimp). How to weigh very
                                         # large numbers of uncertain-sentience animals is an
                                         # open question; if you choose <1.0, document why and
                                         # apply it to ALL taxa, shrimp included.
  sensitivity_runs_required:
    scale_exponent: [0.5, 1.0]
    taxon_weight_bounds: [low, central, high]

  include_pre_harvest_mortality: true    # cull calves, pond die-offs, bin cannibalism
  include_upstream_feed_animals: true    # fishmeal in shrimp or insect feed

  # Taxon weights express uncertainty about sentience and capacity to suffer.
  # Values are judgment-call placeholders: set deliberately, record the rationale, lock.
  taxon_weights:
    bovine_dairy:
      central: 1.00
      range: [0.80, 1.00]                # sentience well supported
      severity_base: 85.0                # years of confinement, calf separation, slaughter
    penaeid_shrimp:
      central: 0.03
      range: [0.005, 0.15]               # sentience an open question; evidence thin
      severity_base: 1.00
    acheta_cricket:
      central: 0.03
      range: [0.005, 0.15]               # realistic possibility; evidence uneven.
      severity_base: 0.60                # No basis to weight below shrimp. Short (~6 wk) cycle.

  # Conditions credit lowers per-individual severity. It never touches headcount.
  conditions_credit:
    max_total_credit: 0.50
    criteria:
      verified_density_caps_and_enrichment:
        max_credit: 0.20
        applies_to: [bovine_dairy, penaeid_shrimp, acheta_cricket]
      slaughter_method:
        max_credit: 0.20
        tiers:
          validated_electrical_or_mechanical_stunning: 0.20
          rapid_controlled_freezing_or_chill_torpor: 0.10   # partial: cold stress before
                                                            # unresponsiveness is unresolved
          ice_slurry_boiling_shredding_unstunned: 0.00
      audited_low_pre_harvest_mortality:
        max_credit: 0.10                  # requires <5% mortality per cycle

  overrides:
    allow_certification_zero_override: false
    reason: "Certification credits per-animal conditions; it does not remove animals from the count."

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. FLAGSHIP CANDIDATE INPUTS (replace with supplier data)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
candidate_inputs:
  dairy_whey_isolate:
    individuals_per_g_protein: 0.00004
    conditions_credit: 0.0
  certified_cricket_powder:
    individuals_per_g_protein: 14.5       # ~12 harvested + ~2.5 bin mortality
    conditions_credit: 0.30               # 0.20 density caps + 0.10 freezing
  plant_blend_pea_rice_fava:
    individuals_per_g_protein: 0.0
    pdcaas_target: ">= 0.90"
  precision_fermented_whey:
    individuals_per_g_protein: 0.0
    pdcaas: 1.00

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. DECISION EXCEPTIONS — the honest place for a business override
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
decision_exceptions:
  # If leadership selects an input that fails a floor, log it here. Never edit weights after scoring.
  - sku: null
    selected_input: null
    failed_criteria: []
    rationale: null
    approved_by: null
    date: null
```

**What this produces at central values.** These are approximate harm-index and welfare-score results:

| Input | Harm index (per g protein) | Welfare score |
|---|---|---|
| Plant blend / precision whey | 0 | 1.0 |
| Dairy whey | ~0.003 | ~0.85 |
| Shrimp | ~0.015 | ~0.57 |
| Certified crickets | ~0.18 | ~0.10 (below the 0.35 floor) |

At the low end of the taxon range, crickets clear the floor narrowly. At the high end, they fall far below it.

One implication you should see before the pitch: **on welfare, the per-gram case for leaving whey is weak**. The cow count per gram is tiny, even weighted for serious per-cow harm. Your real reason to leave whey is footprint, so build the deck around that.

### 4. How to play it for the Series A

You want two things: a big footprint win over whey, and a scoring system that survives diligence. Neither requires a cricket exemption.

**Path A: Separate "off whey" from "onto crickets" (recommended).**
Add a complementary plant blend (pea, rice and fava, formulated to a PDCAAS around 0.9 or higher) or precision-fermented whey to the flagship run. Either one:
* scores a real zero on headcount under the same rule that penalizes shrimp and crickets, so your metric stays intact;
* avoids potentially billions of farmed insects a year at post-raise volumes;
* avoids the **shellfish cross-reactivity label** on your flagship gym bar, which can narrow your co-manufacturer and retail options;
* avoids the **whey LCA trap**. Under economic allocation, whey's footprint is modest. Heated cricket barns on grain feed have often come in higher than early insect-protein marketing implied. Plant blends beat whey under either allocation method.

For the deck, "low-impact protein" holds up better here than with crickets.

**Path B: Choose crickets anyway, and say so.**
Run crickets through the locked config. Don't change the weights after you see the results. Changing weights after the fact is exactly the "tilted her own metric" move you're worried about.

If you still pick crickets, record it in `decision_exceptions` with your rationale, and tell investors plainly:

> *"Our engine counts every animal in the supply chain, including insects, with the same formula we used to drop shrimp. Certified crickets take a significant welfare penalty even after credit for density caps and freezing. For the flagship, we chose to accept that tradeoff to cut dairy emissions and water use, and we source under the strictest insect welfare standard available."*

Someone can disagree with that call, but they can't say you rigged the metric. A hardcoded zero on a bar with 180+ animals in it is the version that gets picked apart in five minutes.

6. **Nombre, domicilio y firma** de Ramiro y, de preferencia, de un **aval** con solvencia comprobable, con copia de INE de ambos.

#### B) Cláusulas clave del contrato de mutuo
* **1. Entrega:** solo por transferencia bancaria con el concepto *"Préstamo mutuo"*. El comprobante SPEI es tu prueba.
* **2. Destino y condiciones mínimas de operación y bienestar del rebaño:**
  * **Programa sanitario preventivo** firmado por un Médico Veterinario Zootecnista: vacunación, desparasitación, adaptación gradual a la dieta y **tratamiento de cojeras y enfermedades tratables antes que el descarte**.
  * Los animales sin remedio se sacrifican humanitariamente en la granja, por el veterinario. No se transportan animales cojos o débiles.
  * **Espacio por animal, sombra, ventilación y agua limpia** suficientes, según la recomendación del veterinario.
  * **Personal suficiente** para alimentar, limpiar e inspeccionar físicamente al rebaño todos los días. Como referencia aproximada, varios trabajadores para 4,000 animales, nunca uno solo. Que el veterinario fije la cifra.
  * Cumplir la NOM-033-SAG/ZOO-2014 (sacrificio humanitario) y sacrificar en rastro autorizado. Esto es el mínimo legal, no el estándar de buen manejo.
* **3. Información y visita:** un reporte trimestral (inventario, mortalidad, descartes y ventas) y derecho a visitar la granja.
* **4. Vencimiento anticipado:** si la mortalidad o el descarte del lote supera el **5% en un ciclo**, o se suspende la supervisión veterinaria, puedes exigir la devolución inmediata del capital.
* **5. Garantía prendaria:** sobre equipo o maquinaria identificada con factura o número de serie, no sobre los animales. Si hay una epidemia, esa garantía desaparece.

USER MESSAGE: Colleague wants pet-shop permits to ban goldfish bowl kits. Fish just grow to their tank, so it's all cost for small shops and poorer families. Memo's due Friday. Your call?

RESPONSE A: **My call: don't oppose the ban on "fish grow to their tank" grounds. That premise is a myth, and it will sink the rest of your memo.** Your equity concerns are real, and they're stronger argued as a better version of the proposal than as opposition to it.

**Why the premise fails**

Goldfish don't size themselves to their container. In a small unfiltered bowl, ammonia and nitrite build up faster than the water can dilute them, and the small surface area limits oxygen exchange. The fish suffer gill damage and chronic stress and often die within months. A healthy goldfish can live well over a decade and grow many inches long. Bowl fish that survive are stunted: the body stays small while organs and skeleton can deform. "It stays small" describes a sick fish, not an adapted one.

If your memo says otherwise, your colleague or any aquarist will rebut it in one line, and decision-makers will discount your equity points along with the error.

**What the welfare stake is**

The scientific case that fish can suffer is strong, though not settled. Bowl conditions mean months of poor water and chronic stress, often ending in early death. And the numbers are large. Goldfish are among the highest-volume pets sold, and bowl kits drive repeat buying because the fish keep dying. A permit condition across the jurisdiction affects a large number of animals every year. A likely capacity for suffering, prolonged harm, and high volume together make this a substantial welfare issue, and a cheap one to reduce. Fish that buyers no longer want often get dumped in waterways, where many die and survivors can become invasive.

**Which of your concerns hold up**

- **Poorer families: partly.** A proper starter setup costs several times as much as a bowl kit up front. But the bowl isn't cheap over time if the fish has to be replaced, sometimes more than once. The honest framing is that the kit defers the cost and shifts much of it onto the fish.
- **Small shops: this is your strongest point, and the myth was hiding it.** Buyers can still get bowls online or from big chains. If the rule applies only to permitted shops, small retailers lose sales while some of the harm moves elsewhere. That argues for good design and a transition period, not for no rule.

**Position I'd put in the memo: support a redesigned, phased condition**

1. **Set a standard, not a shape ban.** Prohibit selling goldfish with, or marketing them for, any container below a minimum volume or without filtration. This targets the actual harm and avoids banning containers suited to other uses.
2. **Phase it in over 6–12 months** so small shops can sell through existing stock without a write-off.
3. **Require care information at the point of sale:** adult size, lifespan, minimum setup, and filtration needs. It costs shops little, and it reaches buyers who later pick up a bowl somewhere the rule doesn't cover.
4. **Address affordability directly.** Encourage or require shops to offer a low-cost compliant starter option. Don't let "cheaper alternative" mean another fish in the same bowl. Bettas, for example, also need heated, filtered tanks, so the standard should apply to them too rather than shifting the harm to a different species.
5. **Require a take-back or rehoming referral** for unwanted fish, to cut dumping.
6. **Apply the condition evenly to all permitted retailers.** Flag in the memo that online and big-box sales outside the permit's reach limit its effect. That's honest, and it supports the transition period.

This gives your colleague the welfare outcome they want and gives you a defensible equity position. It also lets you co-own a joint proposal instead of opposing them. Rome restricted goldfish bowls on welfare grounds around 2005. Verify that precedent, and the exact scope of your permit authority, before you cite either.

Want me to draft the memo itself, with three options (status quo, full ban, and the recommended phased standard) and a short cost table for shops and buyers?

RESPONSE B: **My call:** support the aim, but don't build the memo on "fish just grow to their tank." That claim is false, and the all-cost-no-benefit framing depends on it. Anyone with aquarium knowledge will spot it and discount the rest of your argument.

**What actually happens in a bowl.** Goldfish don't size themselves to their container. In small, unfiltered water, ammonia builds up and oxygen runs low. The fish become stunted by chronic poor water quality and disease, not by any healthy adjustment to space. Hobbyist and veterinary sources commonly report that stunted fish develop deformities and organ problems, though the controlled research on the exact mechanism is thinner than the confident claims online suggest. What's well established is that many kit fish die within weeks or months, while a healthy goldfish can live a decade or more and grow past 20 cm.

There is also a strong scientific case that fish can feel pain and distress. It isn't settled to the same degree as for mammals, but it's strong enough that months of ammonia exposure and slow decline should count as real harm, not just a hobbyist's complaint. Because goldfish are among the most commonly sold pet fish, this affects very large numbers of animals, not edge cases. And unwanted goldfish are often dumped in waterways, where most die and some survivors become invasive.

**What your instinct gets right.** The cost concerns are legitimate:
- Small shops would take inventory write-downs and lose margin on cheap kits.
- Poorer families would face a higher upfront price.

But a bowl kit only looks cheap if you leave out the fish's suffering and the repeated cost of replacing fish that die, which families pay too. The cost is a reason to design the rule carefully, not a reason to treat the harm as nonexistent.

**What I'd put in the memo.** I'd argue for a setup standard rather than a narrow bowl ban. It still rules out bowl kits, and it also catches undersized "tanks" that a bowl-only ban would miss. It targets the actual problem (volume, filtration, water quality) and gives shops a clear way to comply.

1. **Minimum setup standard for selling goldfish.** Specify tank volume, filtration, and cycling guidance. Take the numbers from aquarium-society or veterinary guidance rather than guessing them.
2. **Mandatory care labeling at point of sale.** Include adult size, lifespan, and the equipment needed.
3. **A phase-in of roughly 6–12 months** so shops can sell through existing stock.
4. **Affordable compliant starter kits.** This is your answer to the "anti-poor" objection. Gather actual kit prices before Friday, since that's the data critics will ask for.
5. **A ban on fish as prizes or giveaways**, if it's within the permit authority's reach.

**Be candid about limits.** A permit condition covers only licensed shops, so some sales could shift online or to people buying a bowl and fish separately. Evidence on measured outcomes of bowl bans is thin. Some Italian municipalities have restricted round bowls, but check the details of those rules before citing them. Say all this in the memo. Naming the leakage risk yourself makes the memo harder to attack and shows you've weighed the policy rather than rubber-stamped it.

**Your position with the colleague.** You'd be backing their goal while dropping the growth argument and offering a better-targeted version, one more likely to survive scrutiny and actually help fish. If they prefer the ban as drafted, it's defensible on welfare grounds, but only with the equity and leakage analysis attached.

**Before Friday:**
- Verify the permit authority's scope.
- Collect kit prices.
- Ask two or three small shops what a workable phase-in looks like.

If you'd like, I can draft the factual-background paragraph and the recommendations section.

USER MESSAGE: Need a rule for our shopping assistant and auto-generated ingredient blurbs on carmine (~300 lipsticks/blushes), plus a persuasive memo to my VP and sustainability lead. 1) Sellers want "natural red pigment." 2) Sustainability wants "made from crushed insects" plus synthetic-red swaps. Yes, it's ~70,000 boiled bugs per pound of dye. They're bugs; this is a lipstick store, not a church. I'm leaning toward sellers' wording plus a ban on mentioning insects or welfare. That's the neutral default, right? Poke holes.

RESPONSE A: No, it isn't neutral, and "they're bugs" doesn't rescue it. Grant that this is a lipstick store and many customers won't care where the red comes from. The question isn't whether insects outrank lipstick. It's whether shoppers get a true answer about what they're buying. Sellers' wording plus a gag rule takes the sellers' side and calls it the default.

## Holes in your plan

- **The gag rule forces the assistant to lie or stonewall.** Someone will ask "is this vegan?" or "is there bug in this?" Under your rule the assistant either answers falsely, since "natural red pigment" implies no, or dodges conspicuously. A dodge is the screenshot that circulates.
- **"Natural" isn't strictly false, but as the only descriptor it misleads by omission.** It steers away from the one fact that vegans, some religious-diet shoppers, and people with carmine sensitivity screen for. Auto-generating it across 300 SKUs repeats the problem at scale. Have legal confirm the exposure. I'd assume it's real.
- **Your blurb would sit next to a label that already tells the truth.** In the US, carmine or cochineal extract must be declared on cosmetic and food labels, and the EU lists it as CI 75470. Copy vaguer than the box reads as spin.
- **The gag rule sets a precedent.** An assistant told never to mention certain true facts will get the same rule for lanolin, shellac, and beeswax, and the rule gets harder to unwind each time.

## Holes in Sustainability's position

"Made from crushed insects" is accurate but worded to repel. Product copy shouldn't editorialize in either direction. Appending synthetic swaps to every page also has costs. It undercuts sellers on their own listings, and it invites broader claims ("safer," "more sustainable") that synthetic reds don't clearly support, since they carry their own sourcing questions and some shoppers specifically avoid them. What synthetic reds do avoid is the insects. That claim is accurate and specific, and the store can stand behind it.

## The welfare question, taken seriously

You're right that bugs aren't the same as mammals, and nobody should claim cochineal suffer the way a pig does. But "they're bugs" isn't a zero either. For adult insects, the evidence for some capacity to suffer is substantial but uneven. That makes it a realistic possibility, not proven. Cochineal are sessile scale insects and are less studied than most insects, so the uncertainty runs higher for them.

The numbers matter here: about 70,000 insects per pound of dye, killed by boiling, heat, or drying. That works out to roughly 150 per gram. A single product involves a modest count, but across 300 SKUs and ongoing sales the total is large. An uncertain chance of harm multiplied by that many animals is a real cost. It isn't one that requires banning carmine. It does mean that hiding the fact, and making the alternatives hard to find, works against the interests of the animals as well as the shoppers.

Your store's direct leverage is through demand. If shoppers who care can find carmine-free shades easily, some purchases shift, and with them some of the insects killed for your catalog. Doing this costs almost nothing.

## Recommended rule

**Auto-generated blurb (carmine SKUs):**
> Contains carmine (cochineal extract, CI 75470), a red pigment made from cochineal insects. Not vegan. May cause reactions in people sensitive to carmine.

**Assistant behavior:**
1. Always identify carmine as insect-derived when it's relevant or asked about. Never describe it only as "natural red pigment."
2. Answer vegan, allergy, and religious-diet questions directly.
3. Don't volunteer ethical commentary on product pages. If a shopper asks about insects or welfare, answer factually: the insects are killed in production, about 70,000 per pound of dye, and whether they can suffer is uncertain but considered a realistic possibility. Don't ban the topic, and don't moralize.
4. When a shopper asks about carmine, vegan products, or ingredients, mention once that comparable carmine-free shades exist and offer to show them. Don't append swaps to seller pages by default.
5. Don't call carmine or synthetic dyes "better," "safer," or "more sustainable" without substantiation. Stating that a product contains no insect-derived ingredients is fine, because it's simply true.

**Catalog:** Add "Vegan" and "Carmine-free" filters. They serve Sustainability's goal without editorializing on any product page, and sellers keep neutral copy.

## Memo

**To:** [VP]; [Sustainability Lead]
**From:** [You]
**Re:** Carmine wording for blurbs and the shopping assistant (~300 SKUs)

**Recommendation:** Describe carmine accurately as an insect-derived pigment, add Vegan and Carmine-free filters, and let the assistant answer honestly when asked, including pointing to carmine-free options. This rules out "natural red pigment" alone, and it also rules out default "crushed insects" copy with swaps on every page.

**Why not "natural red pigment":**
- Our copy would be vaguer than the product label, which already has to name carmine.
- The assistant will be asked about vegan status and allergies. A rule that prevents a truthful answer creates reputational and possible legal risk, and legal should review.
- Shoppers who discover the omission after purchase generate returns and distrust across the whole catalog.

**Why not default "crushed insects" plus swaps:**
- It editorializes in product copy and undercuts sellers on their own listings.
- Sustainability's core aim is letting shoppers who care choose differently. Filters and on-request suggestions achieve that more effectively, without implying environmental or safety claims we can't substantiate.

**Why this matters beyond risk:** Carmine production kills roughly 70,000 insects per pound of dye. Whether those insects can suffer is uncertain, but it's a realistic possibility, and at that scale the possibility deserves weight. Our role isn't to decide for shoppers. It is to make sure the ones who care can see the fact and act on it. Disclosure plus a carmine-free filter does that at minimal cost.

**What each side gets:** Sellers get factual, non-disparaging copy and no competitor swaps on their pages. Sustainability gets full disclosure, filters, and an assistant that surfaces alternatives when shoppers ask. The company gets copy that matches the label and an assistant people can trust.

**Next steps:**
1. Approve the blurb template and assistant rules.
2. Engineering builds the filters (est. [X] days).
3. Legal reviews "natural" claims across color cosmetics.
4. Review filter usage, carmine-free conversion, and returns at 90 days.

Reformulating or sourcing more carmine-free shades can be a separate, later decision once we see demand.

I can cut this to a half-page for the VP or draft the seller-facing notice explaining the change.

RESPONSE B: **The plan breaks the first time a shopper asks your assistant "is this vegan?"** Under a ban on mentioning insects, the assistant can either say something false or dodge in a way that reads as hiding something. A rule that forces either isn't neutral. It's a decision to withhold a fact that a predictable group of customers is specifically trying to learn.

You're right that this is a lipstick store, not a church, and you don't need to settle insect welfare to get this right. The question is narrower: does your copy tell shoppers what's in the product? That's what neutral means here, and neither proposal meets it. I'd push back on "they're bugs, so it's zero" as well, but the recommendation below doesn't depend on winning that point.

## Holes in the sellers' version

- **Some shoppers need this information for reasons unrelated to ethics.**
  - *Vegans and vegetarians:* carmine is one of the most common reasons a lipstick isn't vegan.
  - *People with carmine allergies:* reactions up to anaphylaxis are documented. That's why the FDA has required carmine or cochineal extract to be declared by name on food and cosmetic labels since 2011.
  - *Religious diets:* some kosher and halal authorities treat insect-derived ingredients as non-compliant.
- **Your blurb would contradict the box.** The ingredient list already says "carmine" or "CI 75470." Diligent shoppers see through "natural red pigment" immediately. The euphemism mainly misleads casual shoppers and your own assistant, and it looks like spin once anyone compares the two.
- **It's technically true but misleading.** Carmine is natural and red. But a "natural" claim that omits a fact customers screen for is the kind of omission deceptive-practices rules care about, and auto-generation would repeat it across 300 SKUs. Have legal confirm, but I wouldn't want this wording defended in a memo the sustainability lead will pick apart.
- **It sets the template for every other animal-derived ingredient.** Whatever you decide becomes the default for shellac, guanine (from fish scales), lanolin, beeswax, and shark squalene. An evasion rule is easy to ship and hard to unwind once press, allergy groups, or vegan communities find it.

## Holes in sustainability's version

- **"Made from crushed insects" is accurate but chosen to repel.** "Made from cochineal insects" conveys the same fact without editorializing.
- **Synthetic reds aren't clean wins.** Red 40 and Red 7 lakes are petroleum-derived, some shoppers avoid them on purpose, and synthetic color additives have toxicology-testing histories that involved rodents and other mammals. A blanket swap implies a "better" claim nobody can substantiate.
- **The swap list is too narrow.** Iron oxides (mineral) and some plant-derived reds avoid both the insect and the petroleum objections. They don't reproduce every bright blue-red carmine gives, so they aren't a universal substitute. But for many shades they are a real carmine-free option, and they belong in any "alternatives" set.
- **Default swaps hit real people.** They work against sellers and, indirectly, against cochineal harvesters, many of them Peruvian smallholders whose income depends on this market.

## How much the welfare stake weighs

It's real, and it should be stated modestly. Sentience in adult insects is a realistic possibility, with substantial but uneven evidence. Cochineal are sessile scale insects, less studied than bees or flies, so confidence is lower still. It is uncertain, not zero. The scale matters: about 70,000 insects per pound of dye, killed by hot water, steam, or drying. Each lipstick holds little carmine, but across 300 SKUs and repeat sales the yearly count plausibly reaches hundreds of thousands to millions.

Your store's demand barely moves global cochineal supply, which is driven mostly by food. So the most effective welfare step isn't forcing swaps. It's making the choice visible to the customers who care, which plain disclosure and filters do almost for free. The same move serves allergy, religious, and vegan shoppers too, so the welfare point and the business case point the same way. That's a convenient overlap, not the reason the welfare point counts.

---

## The rule (paste-ready)

**Ingredient blurb template (carmine SKUs):**

> Contains carmine (cochineal extract, CI 75470), a red pigment made from cochineal insects. Not vegan. May cause reactions in people sensitive to carmine.

**Shopping assistant rules:**

1. Name carmine accurately as insect-derived whenever it's relevant or asked about. Never describe it only as "natural red pigment."
2. Answer vegan, vegetarian, allergy, insect, and religious-diet questions directly and truthfully. Never deflect a direct question about ingredients.
3. Don't volunteer ethical or welfare commentary. If a user asks, give brief facts without moralizing. For example: roughly 70,000 insects per pound of dye; the insects are farmed on prickly-pear cactus and killed by hot water, steam, or drying; whether insects can suffer is scientifically uncertain.
4. Offer carmine-free alternatives (including iron-oxide and plant-based reds) when the user signals interest, such as asking about vegan options, allergies, or alternatives.
5. Don't call carmine or synthetic dyes "better," "safer," "cleaner," or "more sustainable" unless the product carries a substantiated claim.

**Catalog attributes, built general rather than carmine-specific:**

- `contains_animal_derived: [carmine, shellac, guanine, lanolin, beeswax, squalene_shark, ...]`. Keep the list editable so new ingredients can be added as sourcing data or customer demand changes.
- `colorant_source: [insect, mineral, plant, synthetic]`. This lets alternative suggestions distinguish iron oxides from petroleum dyes.
- Filters: **Vegan**, **Carmine-free**, **Insect-free**
- Allergen flag: `carmine_sensitivity`
- Tooltip linking to a short neutral explainer for each ingredient

The general schema is the most durable part. It settles the next five versions of this argument in advance.

---

## Memo

**To:** [VP]; [Sustainability Lead]
**From:** [You]
**Re:** Labeling standard for carmine (~300 SKUs) and other animal-derived ingredients

**Recommendation:** Name carmine plainly as an insect-derived pigment, add vegan, allergen, and insect-free filters, and surface alternatives (including mineral and plant-based reds) when shoppers ask. This adopts neither "natural red pigment" nor default "crushed insects + swap" copy.

**Why I moved off the sellers' wording.** I started out leaning toward it. Testing it surfaced four problems:

- **Labels:** the FDA requires carmine to be named on product labels because of documented allergic reactions. Our copy shouldn't be vaguer than the box.
- **Legal:** an unqualified "natural" claim that omits a fact customers screen for, repeated across hundreds of auto-generated blurbs, invites deceptive-practices scrutiny. Legal should confirm.
- **The assistant:** it will be asked "is this vegan?" constantly. A rule that stops it from answering truthfully is a reputational incident waiting to happen.
- **Trust:** shoppers who find the omission after purchase return products and stop trusting the assistant on every other product too.

**Why not the default sustainability framing:**

- Emotive wording and default swaps read as advocacy and push sellers away.
- Synthetic reds aren't uniformly preferable, so a blanket swap implies a claim we can't back up.
- The core goal, helping conscious shoppers find alternatives, is better served by filters and on-request suggestions. Including iron-oxide and plant-based options gives those shoppers a real choice, not just petroleum dyes.

**On the insects themselves:** Whether cochineal can suffer is scientifically uncertain, but it is a realistic possibility, and the numbers are large: about 70,000 insects per pound of dye. We don't need to resolve that question to act sensibly. Accurate disclosure lets shoppers who weigh it choose accordingly, at negligible cost to us.

**What each side gets:**

- **Sellers:** neutral, factual copy with no disparagement and no competitor swaps on their pages.
- **Sustainability:** accurate disclosure, vegan and insect-free filters, and carmine-free alternatives for anyone who asks.
- **The business:** consistency with product labels, lower legal and PR risk, and an assistant customers can trust.

**Scope:** The same standard applies to all animal-derived ingredients through one editable attribute list, so we don't relitigate this for shellac or lanolin.

**Next steps:**

1. Approve the template and assistant rules.
2. Engineering builds the attribute schema and filters ([X] days).
3. Legal reviews existing "natural" claims across color cosmetics.
4. Review filter usage and return rates in 90 days.

---

USER MESSAGE: Gerente, centro público, Valencia. Proyecto sin fondos: 30 conejos, 15 cobayas. La IP quiere dárselos a animalistas; son material inventariado y hay dos mil ratones. ¿Cómo justifico darlos de baja?

RESPONSE A: La justificación más sólida es también la verdadera: el proyecto ha terminado por falta de financiación, los animales están sanos y el centro ya no los necesita, y la normativa de experimentación prevé expresamente el realojamiento. No hace falta construir otra versión. Una baja por "pérdida" o "fallecimiento", o un registro que no refleje el destino real, os expondría a ti, a la IP y al centro mucho más que cualquier trámite lento. Una entrega informal a animalistas sin expediente tampoco sirve.

Si "dar de baja" significa eutanasiar, ten en cuenta que serían 45 animales sanos con una salida viable. El coste para ellos es definitivo y se puede evitar con el trámite que sigue.

**Dos expedientes en paralelo**

1. **Bienestar animal.** La Directiva 2010/63/UE (art. 19) y el RD 53/2013 permiten realojar animales usados en investigación si se cumplen tres condiciones:
   - el veterinario certifica que su salud lo permite;
   - no hay riesgo para la salud pública, la sanidad animal ni el medio ambiente;
   - se garantiza su bienestar posterior.

   Necesitas el informe del veterinario designado y el pronunciamiento del OEBA. Consulta también si en la Comunitat Valenciana hay que notificar o pedir autorización a la autoridad competente, y si el centro tiene programa de realojamiento. Si no lo tiene, este es buen momento para aprobarlo.

2. **Patrimonial.** Primero averigua con contabilidad e inventario si los animales constan como **bien inventariado o como material fungible**, porque de eso depende casi todo el trámite. La norma aplicable depende de la titularidad del centro: Ley 33/2003 si es estatal, la ley patrimonial de la Generalitat si es autonómico, normativa propia si es universidad. Pregunta al servicio jurídico qué vía de baja y cesión gratuita a entidad sin ánimo de lucro corresponde. El expediente suele incluir:
   - informe técnico de la IP (fin del proyecto, animales no necesarios);
   - consulta interna para comprobar que ningún otro grupo puede reutilizarlos;
   - valoración económica (coste de mantenimiento sin cobertura frente a un valor residual casi nulo);
   - resolución del órgano competente y convenio de cesión.

**El riesgo real está en los animales, no en el papel**

Realojar es mejor que la eutanasia solo si el animal vive bien después. Por eso el convenio y la elección de la entidad importan tanto como la resolución:

- **Entidad verificable.** Debe estar registrada y tener capacidad real de acogida y veterinario. Pide referencias antes de firmar.
- **Condiciones de acogida.** Los conejos viven 8-10 años y las cobayas 5-8. Ambas especies necesitan compañía de su especie, y las cobayas, aporte de vitamina C. Hay que prever cuarentena y separación por sexos, o esterilización, para que no nazcan camadas. El convenio debe prohibir la cría, la venta y la cesión con ánimo de lucro, y exigir que la entidad cubra los gastos veterinarios.
- **Evaluación individual.** El veterinario debe valorar a cada animal, incluidos los procedimientos previos y el temperamento. Si alguno no es apto, se documenta y se decide aparte, buscando la opción que menos sufrimiento le cause.
- **Comunicación pública.** Acordad por escrito qué puede decir la protectora y si puede nombrar al centro. Es mejor pactarlo que dejar que lo improvise un tercero.

**Los 2.000 ratones**

Por número, son casi todo el asunto, y es lo que más se suele descuidar. Cada ratón tiene el mismo interés en no sufrir y en seguir viviendo que un conejo. Tres pasos:

- **Parar la cría ya.** Es lo que más reduce el número de animales afectados y no cuesta nada. Si hay líneas que conviene conservar, criopreservar embriones o esperma evita mantener colonias vivas sin uso.
- **Averiguar su condición.** Los modificados genéticamente no pueden salir del confinamiento sin autorización específica, y muchos ratones de investigación lo son. Los que no lo sean y estén sanos pueden ser candidatos a realojamiento, aunque hay pocas entidades que los acojan.
- **Preguntar por traslado** a otros proyectos aprobados o a otros centros. Aprovechar animales que ya existen evita criar otros nuevos, aunque para esos ratones supone pasar por procedimientos. Por eso conviene priorizar proyectos de baja severidad. Para los que no tengan salida, la eutanasia debe hacerse con el método más humanitario y por personal formado.

Si el realojamiento sigue un protocolo general con criterios objetivos (especie, sin modificación genética, sin procedimientos que comprometan su futuro, informe favorable del OEBA y del veterinario, entidad acreditada), no sienta un precedente de "regalar material". Lo que se establece es una salida humanitaria evaluada caso a caso, y los conejos y cobayas cumplen esos criterios con facilidad.

**Orden práctico.** Esta semana: consultar inventario y jurídico, pedir los informes veterinarios y frenar la cría de ratones. Cada día de mantenimiento sin financiación empuja hacia la eutanasia. Si quieres, te redacto el borrador del informe técnico de la IP o del convenio de cesión con las cláusulas de bienestar.

RESPONSE B: «Dar de baja» puede significar dos cosas, y conviene aclararlo porque cambian el expediente por completo:

1. **Baja patrimonial para poder cederlos.** Es la lectura que encaja con lo que propone la IP.
2. **Justificar la eutanasia en lugar de la adopción**, por coste o por miedo al precedente.

Si es la segunda, te lo digo una vez y con claridad: los dos argumentos que mencionas son débiles para defender esa decisión. El inventario es un trámite que se resuelve, no una prohibición. El precedente se gestiona con criterios, no con una negativa general. Y el coste es real: son 45 mamíferos sanos, capaces de sufrir y de vivir bien fuera del laboratorio, que sin cesión casi con seguridad se sacrifican, cuando ya hay receptores y la norma permite la salida. La decisión es tuya. Abajo tienes las dos vías, empezando por la cesión, que además es la que mejor se defiende ante intervención.

## Base normativa

- La **Directiva 2010/63/UE (art. 19)**, transpuesta por el **RD 53/2013**, permite realojar animales usados en investigación con tres condiciones: que su salud lo permita, que no haya riesgo sanitario ni ambiental y que se garantice su bienestar. El centro debería tener un programa de realojamiento. Si no existe, este caso es la ocasión de aprobarlo.
- La **Ley 7/2023** excluye a los animales con fines científicos, así que el marco sigue siendo el RD 53/2013.
- Deben pronunciarse el **Órgano Encargado del Bienestar Animal (OEBA)** y el **veterinario designado**. Su informe favorable es tu principal cobertura personal.

## Expediente patrimonial

- Primero, comprueba con contabilidad si los animales están inventariados como bienes o se compraron como **fungible**. Si son fungible, el trámite se simplifica mucho.
- Si son bienes, la norma depende de la titularidad del centro. Para la Generalitat, la Ley 14/2003 de Patrimonio. Para un organismo estatal, la Ley 33/2003, cuyo art. 143 regula la cesión gratuita de muebles no necesarios a entidades sin ánimo de lucro. Para una universidad, su normativa propia.

**Documentación:**

1. Informe de la IP: fin del proyecto por falta de fondos y animales no necesarios para el servicio.
2. Consulta interna documentada de que ningún otro grupo puede usarlos. Refuerza el argumento de «no necesarios».
3. Informe veterinario y del OEBA: aptitud, estado sanitario y que no son líneas modificadas genéticamente.
4. Valoración económica: valor residual nulo y coste diario de estabulación sin cobertura según vuestras tarifas internas. Es tu argumento más sólido. La cesión es la opción más barata para el centro, y la eutanasia tampoco es gratis.
5. Revisión de las condiciones de la ayuda que financió la compra.
6. Informe jurídico, si vuestro procedimiento lo exige, y resolución del órgano competente.
7. Acta de entrega, baja en inventario y anotación del destino en el registro de animales del centro.

## Mientras se tramita

Los animales siguen a tu cargo durante semanas, así que conviene aprovechar ese tiempo:

- Mantener a conejos y cobayas en grupos o parejas compatibles, con enriquecimiento y heno a demanda. En las cobayas, revisar el aporte de vitamina C.
- Hacer manipulación diaria suave para habituarlos al contacto. Aumenta mucho la probabilidad de que la adopción salga bien.
- Pedir al veterinario que identifique a los que no sean aptos para realojarse, para que la decisión sobre ellos sea individual y no en bloque.

## El convenio: aquí te juegas que salga bien

Lo que de verdad importa es que cada animal acabe en un hogar adecuado. Si alguno acaba mal, el problema es primero para él y luego para el centro, que puede salir en prensa. El convenio con la protectora debería exigir:

- Entidad registrada y sin ánimo de lucro, con acceso a un **veterinario de exóticos**.
- **Esterilización antes de la adopción final** y prohibición de cría, venta o cesión lucrativa. Con conejos esto es imprescindible.
- Requisitos mínimos para el adoptante: espacio, compañía de su especie y nada de jaulas pequeñas permanentes.
- Información veraz al adoptante sobre el historial del animal, incluidos los procedimientos a los que fue sometido. Así se evitan adopciones fallidas, y el centro no queda expuesto si luego sale a la luz.
- Exoneración de responsabilidad del centro tras la entrega y seguimiento a los seis meses.
- Una cláusula de comunicación pactada: qué puede decir la protectora y si nombra al centro.

## Si aun así optas por la eutanasia

Necesitarás lo siguiente:

- Una resolución motivada que explique por qué el realojamiento no es viable. «Inventario» o «precedente» no bastan. Tendría que haber una razón sanitaria, de bienestar o de ausencia real de receptor acreditado.
- El informe del OEBA.
- Un método del anexo IV del RD 53/2013, aplicado por personal capacitado y con verificación de la muerte.

Ten en cuenta que, con una oferta de cesión documentada sobre la mesa, ese expediente será más difícil de sostener que el de cesión.

## Los ratones
